ja: だいひゃくじゅうさんかい

p.src: Now, Aunt Zhao had been stricken with a sudden illness at the temple. Seeing that few people were about, she began raving all the more wildly, terrifying and repelling everyone, while two women supported her. Aunt Zhao knelt on both knees, speaking awhile and weeping awhile; at times she crawled on the ground and begged for mercy, crying, “They are beating me to death! My red-bearded lord, I shall never dare do it again.” At other times she clasped her hands together and cried out in pain. Her eyes bulged, fresh blood streamed from her mouth, and her hair hung loose; everyone was terrified and dared not approach. By then evening was drawing on, and Aunt Zhao’s voice grew steadily hoarser until it sounded exactly like the howling of a ghost. No one dared remain near her, so they had to summon several courageous men to sit in the room. Aunt Zhao would appear to die, then revive after a while, and the turmoil continued throughout the night. On the following day she said nothing, but merely pulled grotesque faces and tore open her clothes with her own hands, baring her chest as though someone were stripping her. Pitiful Aunt Zhao could not speak, yet the agony visible in her condition was truly unbearable to behold. At this critical moment a physician arrived, but even he dared not examine her. He merely advised them to “prepare for the funeral,” then rose and made to leave. The servant escorting the physician pleaded with him again and again: “Please, sir, feel her pulse, so that I may report to my master.” The physician felt with his hand and found that her pulse had already ceased. Only when Jia Huan heard this did he burst into loud weeping. Everyone attended only to Jia Huan, and no one saw to Aunt Zhao. Only Aunt Zhou was heartsick, thinking, “This is all the fate that awaits a concubine or secondary wife! And she at least has a son. What will become of me when my own death comes, I wonder!” At this she wept even more bitterly than the rest. Meanwhile, the man hurried back to the house and made his report. Jia Zheng immediately sent servants to make the customary arrangements. They remained with Huan for three days and then all returned together.

p.src: After the man had gone, the story spread from one person to ten and from ten to a hundred, until everyone knew that Aunt Zhao, having maliciously plotted to harm others, had been tortured to death in the court of the underworld. It was also said, “Second Mistress Lian will probably not recover either. Why else would they say that she lodged the accusation?” When these words reached Ping’er, she became deeply anxious. From Xifeng’s condition it truly seemed that she could not recover, while Jia Lian had lately shown none of his former affection toward her. Though he did have many affairs to attend to, he behaved as if her illness had nothing whatever to do with him. Ping’er did her utmost to comfort Xifeng, while reflecting that Ladies Xing and Wang had been home for several days but had only sent servants to inquire after her and had not come to see her in person. This made Xifeng’s heart still more sorrowful. Even when Jia Lian returned, he had not a single tender word for her. By this time Xifeng wished only for a swift death; as soon as the thought entered her mind, every evil spirit descended upon her. She saw Second Sister You emerge from behind the room and gradually approach the bed, saying, “Sister, it has been a very long time since we met. I have missed you terribly, but though I wished to see you, I could not. Now, after much difficulty, I have at last managed to come in and visit you. You have exhausted all your schemes, yet our Second Master is too muddleheaded to appreciate your intentions. Instead, he blames you for acting too harshly, ruining his prospects, and leaving him unable to face anyone now. It makes me indignant on your behalf.” In a daze Xifeng replied, “Now I too regret having been so narrow-hearted. Yet you have forgotten my former wrongs and still come to see me.” Hearing this from beside her, Ping’er asked, “What are you saying, mistress?” Xifeng suddenly came to herself and remembered that Second Sister You was dead; she must have come to claim her life. Awakened by Ping’er, she was frightened but unwilling to reveal what she had seen, so she forced herself to say, “My mind is wandering. I suppose I was talking in my sleep. Massage me a little.” Ping’er went up and began massaging her. Presently a young maid entered and announced, “Granny Liu has come. The old serving women have brought her to pay her respects to mistress.” Ping’er hurriedly stepped down and asked, “Where is she?” The young maid replied, “She does not dare come straight in and is waiting for mistress’s instructions.” Ping’er nodded. Thinking that Xifeng, being ill, would surely not feel like receiving visitors, she said, “Mistress is resting just now. Tell her to wait for the moment. Ask whether she has come on some business.” The young maid said, “They have already asked her, and she has no business. She says she learned that the Old Lady had passed away, but because no one had informed her, she was late in coming.” As the young maid spoke, Xifeng overheard and called out, “Ping’er, come here. She has kindly come to see me; do not treat her coldly. Go and invite Granny Liu in. I should like to talk with her.” Ping’er therefore had no choice but to go out and invite Granny Liu to come and sit with them.

p.src: Xifeng had just begun to close her eyes when she again saw a man and a woman walking toward the kang, as though they meant to climb onto it. Alarmed, Xifeng called to Ping’er, “A man has come from somewhere and run in here!” She called twice, whereupon Feng’er and Xiaohong hurried in and asked, “What do you need, mistress?” Xifeng opened her eyes and looked, but no one was there. Understanding what had happened yet refusing to speak of it, she asked Feng’er, “Where has that wretch Ping’er gone?” Feng’er replied, “Did you not send her to invite Granny Liu in?” Xifeng composed herself for a while and said nothing.

p.src: Just then Pinger came in with Granny Liu and a little girl, asking, “Where is our lady?” Pinger led her to the kang, where Granny Liu said, “My respects to you, my lady.” Xifeng opened her eyes and looked at her; overcome with sorrow, she said, “Granny, how have you been? Why have you waited until now to come? Look, even your granddaughter has grown this big.” Seeing Xifeng wasted to skin and bone and dazed in mind, Granny Liu too was stricken with grief. “My dear lady,” she said, “how can you have fallen so ill in the few months since I last saw you? What a witless old fool I am! Why did I not come sooner to pay my respects?” She then told Qing’er to pay her respects to the lady. Qing’er merely smiled. Xifeng took quite a liking to her and told Xiaohong to look after her. Granny Liu said, “We country folk hardly know what illness is. If we do fall ill, we pray to the gods and make vows; we have never known anything about taking medicine. Could it be that my lady’s illness was caused by some evil influence she encountered?” Pinger thought this talk improper and tugged at her surreptitiously. Granny Liu took the hint and fell silent. Little did they know that her words had accorded perfectly with Xifeng’s own thoughts. Struggling to speak, Xifeng said, “Granny, you have lived a long life, and what you say is true. Concubine Zhao, whom you met before, is dead too. Did you know?” Granny Liu exclaimed in astonishment, “Amitabha! How could someone perfectly well have suddenly died? I remember she had a young son too. What will become of him now?” “What is there to fear?” said Pinger. “He still has his father and the mistress of the house.” Granny Liu said, “My dear girl, you do not understand. However flawed she may have been, the one who died was his own mother. Someone who did not bear him can never be the same.” These words reopened the floodgates of Xifeng’s sorrow, and she began to sob. Everyone gathered round to comfort her.

p.src: Hearing her mother weeping bitterly, Qiaojie went to the kang, took Xifeng’s hand in hers, and began to cry as well. Still weeping, Xifeng asked, “Have you met Granny yet?” “No,” said Qiaojie. “It was she who gave you your name,” said Xifeng. “She is just like a godmother to you. Go and pay your respects.” Qiaojie stepped forward, but Granny Liu hastily took hold of her, saying, “Amitabha! Please do not overwhelm this old woman with such an honor! Miss Qiao, I have not been here for more than a year. Do you still remember me?” “Of course I remember you,” said Qiaojie. I was still little when I saw you in the garden that year. When you came the year before last, I asked you for a cricket kept over from the previous season, but you never gave me one. You must have forgotten.” Granny Liu said, “My dear young lady, I am a muddleheaded old fool. As for crickets, our village is full of them. It is only that you never come to visit us; if you did, it would be easy to give you a whole cartload.” “Then why not take her home with you?” said Xifeng. Granny Liu laughed. “A precious young lady like her, raised wrapped in silk and satin and fed on delicacies—if she came to our place, what could I offer to amuse her, and what could I give her to eat? Would that not be the ruin of me?” She laughed at her own words, then added, “In that case, perhaps I should find the young lady a husband. Our part of the country may be rural, but there are wealthy families there too, with thousands of qing of land, hundreds of head of livestock, and plenty of silver and coin—though, of course, we have no one like the Gold and Jade of this household. My lady may look down on such families, but to us country folk, a rich landowner of that kind is as exalted as someone in heaven.” Xifeng said, “Go and make the proposal. If I approve, I shall give her to him.” Granny Liu replied, “Surely you are only joking. With a mother like you, even the household of some high official might not be deemed worthy of her. How could you possibly give her to a farming family? Even if you consented, the senior ladies above you would never allow it.” Displeased by this talk, Qiaojie went away to speak with Qing’er. The two girls found they had much to say to each other and gradually became friendly.

p.src: Ping'er, fearing that Grannie Liu's endless talk might weary Xifeng, took her by the arm and said, “You mentioned Her Ladyship, but you haven't been to see her yet. I'll go out and have someone take you to pay your respects, so your journey here won't have been in vain.” Grannie Liu made to leave. “What's the hurry?” said Xifeng. “Sit down. I want to ask whether you've been managing well lately.” Grannie Liu thanked her over and over. “If we hadn't had your help, madam—” she said, pointing to Qing'er. “Why, the child's father and mother would both have starved to death. Country folk still have a hard life, to be sure, but now they've managed to acquire several mu of land and sink a well. They grow vegetables, melons, and fruit, and make a fair sum from selling them each year—quite enough to keep themselves fed. These past two years you've often given them clothes and cloth as well, madam, so ours is counted a comfortably situated household in the village. Amitabha! The other day, when the child's father came to town, he heard that your household had been confiscated, madam, and I was nearly frightened to death. Luckily, someone else said it wasn't this house, and only then did I set my mind at ease. Later I heard that the master here had been promoted, and I was delighted and meant to come congratulate you, but farm work covered every field and I couldn't get away. Then yesterday I heard that the Old Lady had passed away. I was threshing beans in the field when the news reached me, and I was so shocked I couldn't even lift the beans. I stayed right there in the field and wept my heart out. I told my son-in-law, ‘I can't worry about any of you now. Whether the news is true or false, I must go into town and see for myself.’ My daughter and son-in-law aren't heartless either. They wept when they heard, and before dawn today they hurried me into town. I didn't know a soul and had nowhere to ask for news, so I came straight to the back gate. When I saw even the door gods pasted over, I had another terrible fright. After I came in, I looked for Sister Zhou but couldn't find her. Then I ran into a little maid, who said Sister Zhou had done something wrong and been driven out. I waited for a long while longer before I met someone I knew and was finally able to come in. I never imagined that you too would be so gravely ill, madam.” As she spoke, tears fell from her eyes again. Ping'er had been waiting impatiently. Without letting her finish, she pulled her away, saying, “You've talked so long that your mouth must be dry, Grannie. Let's go have a bowl of tea.” She led Grannie Liu to sit in the servants' quarters, while Qing'er remained with Qiaojie. “I don't need any tea,” said Grannie Liu. My good girl, have someone take me to pay my respects to Her Ladyship and let me go weep for the Old Lady.” “There's no need to hurry,” said Ping'er. “You won't be able to leave the city today anyway. I hurried you out just now because I was afraid you might speak without thinking and make our mistress cry. Don't take it to heart.”

p.src: “Amitabha!” said Grannie Liu. “I know you were only being thoughtful, miss. But what can be done to cure madam's illness?” “You've seen her,” said Ping'er. “Do you think it is serious?” “God forgive me for saying so,” replied Grannie Liu, “but she doesn't look well to me.” While they were still speaking, they heard Xifeng calling again. By the time Ping'er reached the bedside, Xifeng had fallen silent again. Ping'er was questioning Feng'er when Jia Lian came in. He glanced at the kang without saying a word, then went into the inner room and sat down in a huff. Only Qiutong followed him in. She poured him tea and fussed attentively over him for a while, whispering no one knew what into his ear. Presently Jia Lian summoned Ping'er and asked, “Isn't your mistress taking her medicine?” “She won't take it,” said Ping'er. What are we to do?” “How should I know?” retorted Jia Lian. Bring me the keys from the cabinet.” Seeing that Jia Lian was angry, Ping'er dared not question him. She could only go out and whisper a word in Xifeng's ear. Xifeng said nothing, so Ping'er placed a small casket beside Jia Lian and turned to leave. “Have ghosts called you away?” Jia Lian snapped. If you leave it there, who do you expect to take it?” Suppressing her anger, Ping'er opened the casket, took out the key, and unlocked the cabinet. “What do you want?” she asked. “What have we got?” countered Jia Lian. Driven to tears with anger, Ping'er cried, “If you have something to say, say it plainly! I'd be content even to die!” “Must I spell it out?” said Jia Lian. That earlier trouble was of your making. Now the Old Lady's expenses are still four or five thousand taels short, and my father has ordered me to raise the money against the estate's land accounts. Do you suppose there's anything there? Can we possibly leave the debts outside unpaid? It's my own fault for bearing this title and responsibility! There's nothing for it but to sell the things the Old Lady gave me. Do you object?” Ping'er said not a word. She began taking the things out of the cabinet. Just then Xiaohong came over and said, “Hurry, Sister Ping! Mistress has taken a turn for the worse.” Forgetting all about Jia Lian, Ping'er hurried back. She saw Xifeng clutching wildly at the empty air, seized her hand, and cried out through her tears. Jia Lian came over to look as well. Stamping his foot, he cried, “If it comes to this, it will be the death of me!” As he spoke, tears fell from his eyes. Feng'er came in and said, “Someone outside is asking for Second Master.” Jia Lian had no choice but to go out.

Can we possibly leave the debts outside unpaid?
It's my own fault for bearing this title and responsibility!
There's nothing for it but to sell the things the Old Lady gave me.
Do you object?”
Ping'er said not a word. She began taking the things out of the cabinet.
Just then Xiaohong came over and said, “Hurry, Sister Ping! Mistress has taken a turn for the worse.”
Forgetting all about Jia Lian, Ping'er hurried back. She saw Xifeng clutching wildly at the empty air, seized her hand, and cried out through her tears.
Jia Lian came over to look as well. Stamping his foot, he cried, “If it comes to this, it will be the death of me!”
As he spoke, tears fell from his eyes.
Feng'er came in and said, “Someone outside is asking for Second Master.”
Jia Lian had no choice but to go out.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xifeng grew steadily worse, and Feng'er and the others could not help weeping. Qiaojie hurried in when she heard them. Granny Liu also hurried to the kang, muttered Buddhist invocations, and performed a few rites to drive out the spirits; sure enough, Xifeng improved somewhat. Presently, Lady Wang heard the news from a maid and came over too. Seeing first that Xifeng was calmer, she felt slightly relieved; then, upon seeing Granny Liu, she said, “How have you been, Granny Liu? When did you arrive?” Granny Liu replied, “My respects, madam.” There was no time for particulars; they spoke only of Xifeng's illness. After they had discussed it for some time, Caiyun came in and said, “Master Jia asks for you, madam.” Lady Wang gave Ping'er a few careful instructions and then went away. After her fit, Xifeng now felt clearer-headed. Seeing Granny Liu there and trusting in her prayers to the gods, she sent Feng'er and the others away, had Granny Liu sit beside her pillow, and told her how disturbed her mind was, as though she kept seeing ghosts and monsters. Granny Liu told her which bodhisattvas in their village were efficacious and which temples answered prayers. Xifeng said, “Please pray for me. I have money for whatever offerings are needed.” She slipped a gold bracelet from her wrist and handed it to her. Granny Liu said, “Young mistress, you needn't give me that. When village folk like us make a vow, once the prayer is granted, a few hundred cash is all we spend. There is no need for so much. Even if I go and pray for you, young mistress, I shall only make a vow. When you are well again, you may spend whatever is needed yourself to redeem it.” Xifeng knew that Granny Liu meant nothing but kindness and could not press her, so she kept the bracelet and said, “Granny, I entrust my life to you. My Qiaojie is forever beset by illnesses and misfortunes; I entrust her to you as well.” Granny Liu readily agreed, then said, “In that case, it is still early enough for me to get beyond the city gates, so I shall go now. When you are better, young mistress, we shall go and redeem the vow.” Terrified by the host of vengeful spirits haunting her, Xifeng longed for Granny Liu to go at once and said, “If you will truly take pains for me and I can sleep soundly even once, I shall be grateful to you. Let your granddaughter stay here.” Granny Liu said, “A country child who knows nothing of the world might only say something foolish here. It would be better for me to take her along.” Xifeng said, “You are worrying needlessly. Since we are all one family, what is there to fear? Though we have become poor, feeding one extra person will make no difference.” Seeing that Xifeng was sincere, Granny Liu thought it would suit her to let Qing'er stay a few days and would also save some food at home. She only feared that Qing'er might be unwilling, so it would be better to call her in and ask; if she agreed, she could stay. She therefore spoke a few words to Qing'er.

p.src: Now, Green Bower Hermitage had originally stood on property belonging to the Jia household. When the garden for the Imperial Visit was built, the hermitage was enclosed within it, but its daily provisions and incense offerings had never drawn upon the Jia family's funds. Now that Miaoyu had been abducted, the nun reported the matter to the authorities. She remained there both to await news of the official pursuit of the bandits and because Miaoyu's foundation could not simply be broken up. She merely informed the Jia household of what had happened. Although everyone in the Jia household knew of it, Jia Zheng had only recently died and the family was still deeply unsettled, so no one dared trouble their elders with such supposedly unimportant business. Only Xichun knew the full matter, and she was anxious day and night. Gradually the story reached Baoyu: some said Miaoyu had been carried off by bandits, while others claimed that worldly desire had stirred in her and she had run away with someone. Baoyu was greatly troubled when he heard this. He reasoned that she must have been seized by villains, that a woman like her would never submit, and that she must surely have died rather than yield. Yet since there was no news of her at all, he remained deeply uneasy and sighed from morning to night. He also said, “How could one who called herself an ‘Outsider Beyond the Threshold’ have met such an end!” Then he reflected, “How lively the garden once was! Ever since Second Sister married, some have died and others have wed. I thought that Miaoyu, untouched by worldly dust, would at least remain safe. Who could have known that trouble would suddenly arise, in a fashion stranger even than Sister Lin's death!” From one person his thoughts passed to a second and then a third. As he looked back on them all, the words of Zhuangzi came to mind: all was empty and insubstantial, and those who lived in this world could hardly escape being scattered like windblown clouds. Unable to restrain himself, he burst into loud sobs. Xiren and the others assumed that his madness had returned and tried in every gentle way to soothe and reason with him. At first Baochai did not know the cause either, and she too admonished him. But Baoyu remained sunk in irresolvable melancholy and seemed dazed and distracted besides. Unable to make sense of it, Baochai made repeated inquiries and at last learned that Miaoyu had been abducted and her whereabouts were unknown. She too was saddened, but because Baoyu was tormenting himself, she addressed him sternly and reasonably. She began by saying, “Since Lan returned from the funeral, he has not been attending school, yet I hear that he studies diligently day and night. He is the Old Lady's great-grandson. She always hoped you would grow into a responsible man, and Master Jia worried over you day and night. If you ruin yourself over idle sentiments and foolish passions, what will become of those of us who remain by your side?” Baoyu had no answer. After a while he said, “Why should I meddle in other people's affairs? I merely lament the decline of our family's fortunes.” Baochai said, “There you go again. Master Jia and Lady Wang have always wanted you to become a responsible man and carry on the legacy of your ancestors. Yet you persist in your delusions and refuse to understand. What is to be done with you?” Finding her words uncongenial, Baoyu leaned upon the table and went to sleep. Baochai paid him no further attention. She told Sheyue and the others to look after him, then went to bed herself.

p.src: Seeing that few people were in the room, Baoyu thought, “Since Zijuan came here, I have never spoken a single heartfelt word to her. I have simply left her neglected and lonely, and I feel terribly sorry about it. Besides, she is not like Sheyue or Qiuwen, whom I can readily find a place for. I remember that when I was ill, she stayed here with me for quite a long time. Even now, that little mirror of hers is still in my keeping; she has certainly shown me no small affection. Yet now, for some reason, she is cold whenever she sees me. If it is on account of the one I married, Zijuan was closest to Cousin Lin, and as far as I can see, she too treats Zijuan quite well. Whenever I am away from home, Zijuan chats freely with her, but as soon as I return, Zijuan withdraws. It must be because Cousin Lin died and I then went ahead and married. Ah, Zijuan, Zijuan! You are such an intelligent girl—can you truly not see even this little share of suffering in my heart?” Then another thought came to him: “Tonight some of them are asleep and the others are busy sewing. I had better take this chance to find her and see what she has to say. If I have offended her in any way, I can at least apologize.” Having made up his mind, he quietly left his room and went in search of Zijuan.

p.src: Zijuan’s small room was in the inner part of the west wing. Baoyu stole quietly up beneath her window. Seeing that a lamp was still burning inside, he moistened the window paper with his tongue and broke a small hole in it. Peering through, he saw Zijuan sitting alone beside the lamp, doing nothing and staring blankly ahead. Baoyu called softly, “Sister Zijuan, are you still awake?” Zijuan gave a start. After sitting stunned for some time, she finally asked, “Who is it?” “It is I,” said Baoyu. Thinking the voice sounded like Baoyu’s, Zijuan asked, “Is that Second Master Bao?” Outside, Baoyu answered softly that it was. “What have you come for?” Zijuan asked. Baoyu said, “There is something in my heart that I want to tell you. Open the door and let me sit with you for a while.” After a pause, Zijuan said, “Whatever you wish to say, Second Master, it is late now. Please go back, and we can speak tomorrow.” At these words, Baoyu’s heart turned half to ice. He still wanted to go in, but feared that Zijuan would not open the door. He considered returning, yet her words had stirred the hidden anguish in his heart more strongly than ever. With no other choice, he said, “I have nothing more to say. I only want to ask you one question.” “If it is only one question,” said Zijuan, “then please ask it.” But Baoyu remained silent for a long while. Hearing no answer from Baoyu, Zijuan remembered his old tendency toward lovesick madness. She feared that if she rebuffed him too sharply, she might bring on his former illness again. So she rose and listened carefully, then asked, “Have you gone, or are you still standing there like a fool? Why will you not say what you came to say? You only stand there tormenting people. You have already tormented one person to death—must you torment another to death as well? Why cause such misery?” As she spoke, she peered out through the hole Baoyu had made and saw him standing there, listening in a daze. Zijuan felt unable to say any more and turned back to trim the candlewick. Suddenly she heard Baoyu sigh and say, “Sister Zijuan, you were never so hard-hearted before. Why is it that lately you will not say even one kindly word to me? I know that I am a foul, unworthy creature, undeserving of any notice from you. But if I have done something wrong, I only beg you to tell me plainly. Even if you never speak to me again for the rest of your life, at least when I die, I shall die knowing why!” Zijuan gave a cold laugh. “So that is what you wished to say, Second Master? Is there anything else? If that is all, I heard such words so often while our young mistress was alive that they became wearisome! If there is anything unsatisfactory about us, I was sent here by Her Ladyship, so you should report me to her. In any case, we servant girls no longer count for anything.”

p.src: As Baoyu stood there grieving, he suddenly heard someone behind him take up the conversation: “Whom are you asking to speak for you? What claim does anyone have on anyone else? If you have offended someone, plead with her yourself. Whether she deigns to forgive you is up to her; why drag insignificant people like us in to bear the brunt of it?” These words startled both the person inside and the one outside. And who do you suppose it was? None other than Sheyue. Baoyu felt thoroughly embarrassed. Sheyue went on: “What is all this about, anyway? One of you apologizes, and the other pays no attention. You had better plead with her quickly. Oh, Sister Zijuan is being much too hard-hearted too! It is bitterly cold outside, and though he has been begging for so long, you have not given the slightest sign of a response.” Then she said to Baoyu, “The Second Mistress was asking for you just now. At this late hour she supposed you were over there, yet here you are standing alone under the eaves! What are you doing?” From inside, Zijuan replied, “What is the meaning of this? I have been asking Second Master to go in; whatever there is to say can wait until tomorrow. Why put yourself through this?” Baoyu wanted to say more, but with Sheyue there he could not speak of anything else. He had no choice but to walk back with her, saying as they went, “Enough, enough! In this life I shall never be able to lay bare what is in my heart! Heaven alone knows the truth!” At these words, tears welled up from some unknown source and streamed down without cease. Sheyue said, “Second Master, take my advice and give up. It is a pity to waste your tears for nothing.” Baoyu made no reply and went into his room. He saw that Baochai was asleep, though he knew she was only pretending. Xiren alone remarked, “Could you not have said whatever it was tomorrow? You had to rush over there and make a scene, and if it had caused—” She stopped there, unwilling to finish. After a pause she continued, “Do you feel unwell anywhere?” Baoyu said nothing and merely shook his head, whereupon Xiren helped him settle down for the night. Needless to say, he did not sleep all night.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zijuan, stirred by Baoyu’s appeal, felt more distressed than ever and wept straight through the night. Turning everything over in her mind, she thought, “As for Baoyu’s marriage, everyone knew he could understand nothing while he was ill, and so they brought it about with all their tricks and deceptions. When Baoyu later came to his senses, his old illness returned, and he often wept and yearned for her; he is no heartless man who has forgotten his love and betrayed his devotion. His tenderness today makes it still harder to bear; our Miss Lin truly lacked the good fortune to receive such love. Seen in this light, every bond in human life is predetermined; before it has run its course, we are all lost in foolish hopes. When at last nothing can be done, the unfeeling cease to care, while those of deep affection and steadfast devotion can do no more than shed bitter tears before the wind and moon. Pitifully, the dead may know nothing of it, while the living truly suffer anguish and heartbreak without end. All things considered, it would be better to be grass, wood, or stone—without knowledge or feeling, and therefore with a heart untroubled!” When her thoughts reached this point, the aching fervor in her heart suddenly turned cold as ice. Just as she was preparing to sleep, she heard a commotion break out in the eastern courtyard. What had happened remains to be told in the next chapter.
